title: Four Symbols That Are Just Handwriting
thesis: The ampersand is the Latin word et, the pilcrow is the letter C for capitulum, the percent sign is the Italian per cento, and the dollar sign is the Spanish abbreviation for pesos. None of the four was designed. Each is a word somebody stopped bothering to finish, in four trades seventeen centuries apart - and the last one is recent enough that the page it happened on is still in an archive.

author.note: Written directly rather than by a subagent, following the drawn-explainer skill as published.

sourcing.primary: Florian Cajori, 'The Evolution of the Dollar Mark', Popular Science Monthly 81 (December 1912) 521-530, and A History of Mathematical Notations vol. 2 (1929) §§402-409. This is the episode's load-bearing source and it is a review-and-reject paper in exactly the sense episode 7 set as the bar: Cajori enumerates eight competing accounts of the $ - the U-over-S monogram, the Stars and Stripes joke made of it, the IHS monogram, the Roman HS/IIS for sestertius, the Potosi mint monogram, the Pillars of Hercules with their ribbon, the several figure-8 theories, and D for dollar - and rejects each against manuscript evidence before arguing for the Spanish ps abbreviation for pesos.
supporting: Ampersand: the et-ligature is attested in Roman cursive from the 1st century CE, the earliest known example being a Pompeian graffito. The form history was catalogued by Jan Tschichold, Formenwandlungen der et-Zeichen (1953), translated 1957 as The Ampersand: Its Origin and Development, with 288 forms. The modern glyph is close to the Carolingian minuscule ligature.

Pilcrow: a C for Latin capitulum, crossed by one or two vertical strokes by rubricators, the bowl later closed and filled. Standard in the palaeographic literature - M. B. Parkes, Pause and Effect: An Introduction to the History of Punctuation in the West (University of California Press, 1993) is the scholarly treatment of the paraph.

Percent: David Eugene Smith identified the 'pc' with a small raised loop - the Italian -o ending, as in primo, secondo - in pages added around 1435 to a 1425 arithmetic manuscript, and traced 'per cento' through 'per 100' and 'p cento'. The abbreviation had become a horizontal fraction mark by about 1650, with 'per' dropped, a form Smith reproduces from a 1684 arithmetic in Rara Arithmetica; the solidus form is modern.
sourcing.whyThisIsNotFolkEtymology: Three independent kinds of support, and the film leans hardest on the one with the strongest evidence. (1) Cajori's method is negative before it is positive: he says of the U-over-S theory that Robert Morris's own letters show a single down-stroke where the letter U would require two, and of the Potosi monogram that the peso abbreviations predate the mint. He reports examining thousands of manuscripts and finding no connecting links for the theories he rejects. (2) For the dollar there is a single document that contains both states at once - Oliver Pollock's 1778 letter survives in two contemporaneous copies, one carrying the flourished ps and the other the mark we now use. That is not a resemblance somebody noticed later; it is the transition itself, dated and attributed. (3) The ampersand's source is physically attested rather than reconstructed: the E and T are still separable in the 1st-century cursive and in every Carolingian and italic form since. The percent chain is the weakest of the four and is treated as such - it gets the shortest thread and the film says the letter was dropped rather than claiming it turned into anything.
refused: '$ is a U over an S, for United States' - the popular account, and the first thing Cajori rejects. The film puts it on screen and crosses it out rather than leaving it unaddressed, because a viewer who arrives believing it will not hear anything else until it is dealt with.

'$ is the Pillars of Hercules with their ribbon, off the Spanish pillar dollar' - also crossed out on screen. Cajori's objection is that no manuscript shows a merchant copying coin imagery into a ledger.

'@ is a ligature of Latin ad', considered for the fourth thread and dropped. The arroba reading is attested from 1536 but the ad-ligature derivation is not settled, and Giorgio Stabile's amphora claim is contested. A contested derivation fails gate 2 whichever way it is animated.
'Rx is the eye of Horus' - the skill names this as a folk-etymology trap and it is one. Not used.

'# is a barred lb for libra pondo' - probably true and reasonably well attested, but dropped on gate 4 rather than gate 2: the source is three strokes and the mark is four, and there is no honest way to split one of them.

'+ is a contraction of et', which would have rhymed beautifully with the ampersand and made the film's turn for free. Refused on gate 4: a cursive et cannot be indexed onto a cross without either a merge or a retrace that reads as a zigzag, and Cajori himself only reports the derivation as generally believed rather than demonstrating it.
Any claim that the pilcrow's bowl was closed on a particular date or by a named hand. The sequence is documented; the moment is not, and the film says 'a monk' and stops there.

gates.drawable: Four morphs, all continuous, all interpolated geometry: a joined cursive et whose t leans back through the e until the pair is an ampersand; a C closing onto the rule drawn through it and flooding red; a p withdrawing along its own abbreviation stroke while a c and a raised o become two zeros; and a p whose bowl collapses onto its stem while the raised s drops over it full size.
gates.trueNotFolk: See sourcing. For the dollar the scholarly account and the popular account point in opposite directions, and the film takes the scholarly one and says so on screen.
gates.genuinelyDifferentShapes: No shot is a tidy-up. The et is the largest: a legible two-letter word becomes a single abstract mark, with the t rotating about 50 degrees and the e pinching from a closed loop into an epsilon. The pilcrow is the arc-tension move - a C whose ends walk onto the rule until the bowl is closed - plus a fill, which is a different event from a fade. The percent's letter lies down into a line. There is no deliberate non-morph in this episode; episode 6 spent that card and episode 7 did not take it back.
gates.topology: Every mark holds a fixed part count and a fixed anchor count in every state, and every corresponding run is indexed the same way round. The et is two strokes throughout (9 and 5 anchors) - the e's exit stroke is the t's crossbar, which is the pen lift the ligature saves and the reason the finished ampersand has no crossbar left to account for. The pilcrow is two throughout (8 and 2). The percent is four throughout (8, 2, 8, 8), with the p ending collinear with the rule rather than fading, so nothing is removed. The dollar is two throughout (8 and 7). All arcs - the C, the c of cento, the raised o and the circles they become - are swept with decreasing angle; ring() in the kit sweeps the other way, so they are built by hand rather than borrowed.

pipeline.narration: SyncVoice (Gemini native audio, voice Kore) via D:/Projects/Utilities/textToSpeechUsingRateLimitlessTTS
pipeline.music: Lyria RealTime (models/lyria-realtime-exp), 163s bed, sidechain-ducked under the voice
pipeline.render: resvg + 24 worker threads -> libx264, 4743 frames in 43s (49s wall including the audio mux)

musicPrompt: Sparse solo harp, plucked softly and damped by hand, played very slowly with wide space between the notes and no repeating melody. A low bassoon holding long quiet tones underneath. Faint dry room tone, like a copying room. Curious and patient, a little old, never grand or ceremonial. Instrumental only, no vocals, no drums, no melodic hook that competes with a speaking voice.

qa.method: Whisper transcript per shot diffed against the script, before any drawing
qa.result: clean; 357 script words, 357 heard, the only remaining differences being number normalisation - 'nine hundred' to '900' in s05, 'seventeen seventy eight' to '1778' in s11, 'seventeen' to '17' in s13. Those three are why every beat in this film is cued on the word timing.json holds rather than the word the script holds.
defectsFound: s10: the entire clause 'second letter raised above the first' was dropped and came out as the single syllable 'cesses'. Six words gone, and it was the only description of the source drawing in the shot - the picture would have had nothing to stand on.
qa.fix: s10 was rewritten from a bare apposition ('Clerks wrote the plural short, second letter raised above the first') to a proper participial clause ('Clerks abbreviated the plural, raising the second letter above the first'), which is what Gemini could hold. One TTS call, one shot re-aligned with align.py s10.peso; the other thirteen shots were never re-transcribed. The re-alignment came back 26 words for 26 and the film gained 2.3s.

notes.budget: 357 words over 14 shots estimated 157.9s against a 145-170s band. Actual speech came in at 146.6s and the film at 155.8s before the s10 fix and 158.1s after - the estimate was 1.3% high. Kore ran at 2.43 words/second, the middle of its measured range.
notes.craft7: Every stage keeps its source on the page at low opacity with a dashed tie to the mark it became. Nothing in this film fades to zero. The percent shot is the one that could have: the honest thing there is that the letter was dropped and the line stayed, and rather than fade the p out it is walked onto the rule's own anchors, so it is still drawn, still four strokes, and simply indistinguishable from the line it lay down on.
notes.rhyme: A grey line under the recap - 'a treble clef did the same thing to a letter G' - pays off for anyone who saw episode 4, where a letter stopped looking like a letter for exactly this reason, and reads as a passing aside for anyone who did not.
notes.turn: Shot 9. The first three derivations have to be reconstructed across centuries; the fourth has a dated page and a named man, so the screen puts the archive reference up - Draper Collection 38J, Wisconsin Historical Society - which the voice never reads. It turns the film from a claim into evidence at exactly the halfway point, and it is where the sourcing stops being something in this file and becomes something on screen.
notes.newInLib: Nothing. travel(), detach(), along(), smooth(), morph() and flood() covered every shot as published.

toolchainFeedback.travel: Fitted three of the four threads without argument and the per-stage from/to really is the lever the note says it is. Two of the three sources here are about 410px across - the joined et reaches a long way right because of the exit stroke, and p-c-o is three marks in a row - and at the usual 660/1320 the travelling copy was still shoulder to shoulder with its own ghost at e≈0.45, so the et stage rendered as 'etEt'. Widening to 540/1420 and taking shrink down to 0.8 opened a real gap; the narrow dollar was fine on the defaults. What travel() still cannot do is ink the mark on: it hands the draw function an opacity and nothing else, so the only way to make a source arrive is to fade it up, which is a pop by another name. The fix was to give each strip generator a `draw` parameter that staggers ink() across its strokes, which is better than an opacity ramp anyway because handwriting should arrive stroke by stroke - but every episode is going to rediscover it. A `draw` argument alongside `opacity` in travel()'s callback contract would be the right home for it.
toolchainFeedback.detach: Exactly right for the pilcrow and it is the only thing that would have worked. The letter is a C in the margin of a page somebody is already writing, at the margin's size; it cannot slide sideways to make room without undoing the shot, because the whole point is that it was made in the middle of other work. The copy growing from 0.56 to 1.32 scale and travelling diagonally to the upper right, with the column thinning where it stands, is the shot. One thing to watch: its ghost default of 0.3 multiplies against whatever opacity the parent already draws itself at, so a faint parent goes to nothing - the column here was drawing at 0.44 and ended up at 0.13, invisible. Raised to 0.42.
toolchainFeedback.stripsAsSource: scene.mjs imports every generator from the four strip modules and not one coordinate is copied. Three design errors were caught on the strip that would each have cost a full render: the cursive e read as a C until its eye was tucked inside the loop and its exit raised to x-height; the et's exit stroke was crossing the t at the foot rather than at the crossbar, which is the whole ligature argument; and both p's had bowls that stopped in mid-air, so smooth() closed them as triangles - a p needs its bowl to land back on the stem as a real anchor. The percent's p was rebuilt three times on the strip, which cost about four minutes and no renders.
toolchainFeedback.alignSubset: align.py s10.peso re-transcribed one shot in about fifteen seconds. With a dropped-clause defect this is the difference between one cheap confirmation and re-running the whole film's alignment to check a single line.
toolchainFeedback.budgetFormula: Trustworthy. 157.9s estimated, 158.1s delivered - 0.1% out, closer than episode 7's 2.7%. Its job here was confirming that a 357-word draft was safe to spend fourteen TTS calls on rather than trimming one.
skillGaps: The topology gate is stated as a property of the finished mark, but in practice it is a constraint on the PEN PATH, and that is a much harder thing to satisfy than equal counts. The percent's source is a medieval per-abbreviation - a p with its descender slashed - and no ordering of eight anchors draws it as one continuous stroke, because a real hand lifts the pen to cross a descender. Every ordering zigzagged. The fix was to let the rule be its own stroke, which then turned out to be the better shot anyway, since a separate rule is a thing that can survive the letter. Worth saying in the gate: if a source cannot be drawn without a pen lift, the lift is a part, and counting it as one usually improves the argument rather than compromising it.

craft.md says 'nothing pops in, everything arrives by ink()', and travel()/detach() do not let you honour it. Their draw callbacks take an opacity, so a source arriving inside one of them fades up unless the episode threads a draw parameter through its own generators by hand. Episode 7's star has the same issue - it is gated on `drawn <= 0 ? '' : travel(...)`, which is a hard cut when the ramp crosses zero. This should be in the traps list or fixed in the kit.

The rule 'cue anything that must stay on screen from a word in the shot's first half' is right and is easy to violate while feeling careful, because the natural cue word for a caption is usually the one that names it - and naming usually comes late in a sentence. Four labels in this film were cued on their obvious word and appeared for the last second of a twelve-second shot. --preview at 82% catches it, which is worth saying explicitly: the late frame is not only for beats that never landed, it is for beats that landed too late to be seen.

Nothing in the skill warns that a label placed below the reveal captions will run off the bottom of the card. The drawing area is roughly y 200-950; a second row of text at y 1000 is outside the paper. A stated safe box would save a render.

youtube.title: These four symbols are not symbols. They are words.
youtube.description:
The ampersand is not a symbol meaning 'and'. It is the Latin word for and - et - written joined up by somebody in a hurry, until the two letters stopped being letters. The oldest one we have is scratched on a wall in Pompeii.

The same thing happened three more times. A monk writing capitulum, Latin for chapter, put down its first letter and ruled a line through it; the rubricator filled the bowl in with red and it closed for good, and that is the paragraph mark. A Florentine merchant reckoning interest by the hundred cut per cento down to a letter, a rule and a raised ending - the letter went, the rule stayed, and a line in a fraction is still read as 'per'. And Spanish-American clerks abbreviated pesos with the second letter raised above the first, until the loop of the p disappeared and left its down-stroke standing through the s.

You were probably told the dollar sign is a U laid over an S for United States. Florian Cajori went through thousands of these manuscripts looking for that letter and never found it, and he disposed of seven other theories the same way. In 1778 a merchant named Oliver Pollock sent one letter out in two copies - one still carries the loop, the other carries the mark we use now.

Sources: Florian Cajori, 'The Evolution of the Dollar Mark', Popular Science Monthly 81 (1912) and A History of Mathematical Notations vol. 2 (1929). Jan Tschichold, The Ampersand: Its Origin and Development (1953/1957). D. E. Smith, Rara Arithmetica. M. B. Parkes, Pause and Effect (1993).

Not Arbitrary: things that look like meaningless convention, shown to be pictures.

tiktok.caption: The ampersand is not a symbol for the word and. It IS the word - et, in Latin, written joined up until the letters gave way. Three more on your keyboard did the same thing.
tiktok.hook: First 3 seconds: a handwritten 'et' with the t leaning back through the e until it is an ampersand.
